content: The personality traits others recognize in us may also have roots in our DNA, with research uncovering genetic connections that go beyond how we see ourselves. Could your DNA help explain why you are naturally outgoing, highly organized, or more prone to worrying than others? A large international study suggests that some of the personality traits that make us who we are may be partly rooted in our genes, raising a fascinating question about how much of our personality is determined before we are even born. Researchers at the University of Tartu have identified more than 1,000 genetic variants associated with human personality in a study involving more than one million people. Published in the journal Nature , the findings offer new insight into how genetics contributes to differences in personality, while also showing why DNA alone cannot explain who we become. The DNA of two randomly selected people is approximately 99.9% identical. Differences in the remaining 0.1% help influence characteristics such as appearance, disease risk, and responses to medication. The new research suggests that these small genetic differences are also associated with five major dimensions of personality: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism. Scientists have known for decades that both genetics and life experiences influence personality. Finding the specific genetic differences involved has been much more difficult because personality is shaped by many genes, each contributing an extremely small effect. Detecting those subtle patterns requires enormous amounts of data. Between 2021 and 2022, the Estonian Biobank gathered personality information from nearly 80,000 participants. Although substantial for Estonia, that sample was not large enough to reliably identify many of the genetic associations researchers were looking for. The University of Tartu team therefore combined its findings with 45 other international datasets, creating a more geographically diverse study population. For certain personality traits, the researchers could analyze data from as many as 1.1 million people. The Estonian sample was the third-largest of all participating groups and used the most comprehensive personality questionnaire. The genetic associations were remarkably consistent across different populations, including people of varying ages and geographical backgrounds. However, the identified variants explained only about 4.8% to 9.3% of the differences in personality traits. That relatively small proportion highlights how much remains unexplained. Social relationships, environmental influences, and personal experiences may all play substantial roles, along with the ways these factors interact with a person’s genetic makeup. One particularly interesting feature of the Estonian research allowed scientists to examine personality from two perspectives. Participants could evaluate their own personalities and invite someone who knew them to provide an independent assessment. “No other biobank in the world offers such an opportunity!” said Uku Vainik, Professor of Behavioral Genetics at the University of Tartu. This approach helped researchers address an important question about personality research. Are genetic associations connected to characteristics that other people can actually observe, or do they mainly reflect how individuals think about themselves? The researchers found substantial overlap between the genetic signals associated with self-reported personality traits and those identified through assessments by acquaintances. “This shows that measurable personality traits are truly real, publicly observable characteristics of people, rather than merely individuals’ own opinions about themselves,” explained René Mõttus, Professor of Personality Psychology and co-lead of the study. The findings are also opening new avenues for understanding the relationship between personality and physical health. Kerli Ilves, a junior research fellow, is investigating whether personality traits may have causal connections to health-related behaviors, including those associated with body weight, smoking, and alcohol consumption. Her preliminary findings suggest that personality could influence these behaviors, although the relationship may also work in the opposite direction. Established behavioral patterns might themselves contribute to changes in personality over time. “We especially see this kind of relationship in smoking,” Ilves noted. Researchers emphasize that these early findings do not yet establish cause and effect. Understanding whether personality shapes health habits, whether those habits alter personality, or whether both processes occur will require additional research. “The next step is to use other methods, such as longitudinal studies, to determine whether changes in personality are accompanied by changes in health behavior, and vice versa,” explained Vainik. The Estonian Biobank is planning another study focused on personality and cognitive functioning. By examining how personality develops and interacts with everyday behavior, researchers hope to better understand what influences people’s health choices and eventually support more effective, personalized approaches to healthy living. content: A technology older than the laser is finding new life inside diamond, offering a potential way to make quantum computers more powerful without overwhelming their sensitive measurement systems. A quantum computer can process information using the strange rules of quantum physics, but getting an accurate answer out of it presents a challenge. The information is carried by extremely faint microwave signals that must be amplified before they can be measured. Unfortunately, amplifying those signals can introduce unwanted noise, making it harder to tell what the computer is actually saying. Researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have developed a new amplifier that tackles this problem using an unlikely material: diamond. Their device can strengthen microwave signals more than 1,000 times while adding very little noise. It can also handle stronger signals and operate in magnetic fields, potentially overcoming limitations that make today’s quantum computers difficult to scale up. The findings were published on November 16, 2026, in Nature Communications . In superconducting quantum computers, information is stored in quantum bits, or qubits. To determine a qubit’s state, researchers measure a weak microwave signal associated with it. The difficulty is that these signals are extraordinarily sensitive to interference. That is one reason superconducting quantum computers operate at temperatures close to absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. Keeping the equipment this cold reduces interference caused by heat, but it cannot eliminate the noise introduced by the amplifiers themselves. Once that unwanted noise enters the measurement, subsequent amplification stages strengthen it along with the original signal, increasing the chance of an incorrect reading. Existing amplifiers can detect these faint signals with remarkably little added noise, although they come with trade-offs. Conventional Josephson parametric amplifiers, for example, can become overwhelmed when several qubits are measured simultaneously. This effect, known as saturation, limits how many signals they can reliably process at once. Another technology, known as kinetic inductance parametric amplification, can handle stronger signals but generally requires more electrical power and additional wiring. As quantum computers grow, that extra equipment adds cost and complexity. Some systems also use qubits based on electron spin, which require magnetic fields that can disrupt conventional superconducting amplifiers. The OIST researchers approached these challenges by revisiting a technology that predates the laser. Masers were first demonstrated in 1954, six years before lasers appeared. Both technologies amplify electromagnetic waves, but while lasers work with light, masers operate with microwaves. They rely on a process called stimulated emission, in which an incoming photon carrying the right amount of energy prompts an excited electron to release another matching photon. Repeating this process strengthens the original signal. “Despite being invented before optical lasers, masers — microwave lasers — have been left far behind because they often require cryogenic conditions to function, which made them impractical until very recently,” explains Dr. Yuimaru Kubo, head of the Hybrid Quantum Device Team at OIST. “But now, with quantum computers operating at temperatures very close to absolute zero, we have given them new life as very promising candidates for amplifying quantum signals with very little noise.” To put this older technology to work, the team used a specially prepared diamond containing nitrogen impurities known as P1 centers. These impurities contain electrons whose spin, an intrinsic quantum property, makes them behave like tiny magnets. The researchers apply a relatively weak microwave field to the diamond, supplying energy that pushes most of these electron spins into higher-energy states. When a faint microwave signal enters the amplifier, it stimulates the excited spins to release their stored energy as additional microwaves at the same frequency. In effect, the diamond transfers energy from its excited electrons into the incoming signal, making that signal stronger without requiring a powerful microwave source. “We were surprised by how much amplification we could achieve using such a small amount of microwave power,” adds Kubo. In testing, the diamond maser amplified microwave signals more than 1,000-fold while introducing just 2.55 quanta of added noise. Quanta are discrete units used to describe energy at the quantum scale. For comparison, the fundamental quantum limit for this type of amplification is 0.5 quantum, meaning that even an ideal amplifier cannot eliminate added noise entirely. The device also tolerated much stronger incoming signals than conventional Josephson parametric amplifiers. Because the diamond maser operates in a magnetic field, it could be particularly useful for quantum computers that rely on spin-based qubits. Although the technology is still being developed toward commercialization, its potential uses extend beyond quantum computing. Sensitive microwave amplification is also important in spectroscopy, which scientists use to investigate the properties of materials, and nuclear magnetic resonance, the physical principle behind MRI scanners. Other possible applications include fundamental physics experiments searching for dark matter, where detecting extremely weak signals could help researchers investigate one of the universe’s most elusive mysteries. Reference: “A near-quantum-limited diamond maser amplifier operating at millikelvin temperatures” by Morihiro Ohta, Ching-Ping Lee, Vincent P. M. Sietses, I. Kostylev, J. R. Ball, P. Moroshkin, T.
